letters-of-ulysses-s-grant-to-his-father:
Ulysses S. Grant's letters to his father and youngest sister cover 1857 to 1878. His nephew, Jesse Grant Cramer, edited the volume in 1912. Portraits of Grant and his parents illustrate it.

A facsimile shows Grant's handwriting in a letter to his father. Jesse Root Grant, his father, appears aged sixty-nine in one portrait. The letters span Grant's lean years, war command, and presidency. Family duty and plain honesty mark his tone throughout. Readers meet the famous general as a son and brother at home. Jesse Grant, his father, was a tanner and businessman. The son's respect for him runs through every letter.
life-of-st-francis-of-assisi:

nasa-tm-19640019313-engine-integrated-se:
William J. D. Escher and Donald D. Thompson of Marshall wrote this report. It studies steering a hydrogen rocket without swinging the whole engine. The method injects gas into the exhaust jet from the side. That side push is called secondary injection side-force in the title.

The abstract calls the idea a strong alternative to gimbaling big engines. Large hydrogen engines are heavy, and swinging them takes strong gear. The report analyzes how the side injection works in detail. It also reviews past work, noting a lack of hydrogen-focused effort. Marshall had hired out a program to fill that gap with hard data.
nasa-tm-19660024081-on-the-general-pertu:
Peter Musen, of the Theoretical Division at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper on how planets disturb each other's paths. In a planetary system, every planet pulls on the others with gravity. Those pulls slowly shift each planet away from the simple oval orbit it would follow alone.

Musen builds a general theory of these shifts, called perturbations. He expands the change in each planet's position vector into a series. The series is arranged by powers and products of the planets' masses. That form lets astronomers compute positions step by step, including the small effects that simpler orbit math leaves out.
nasa-tm-19670009030-payload-to-mars-reco:
C. A. Wagner, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this report, issued February 1967. It answers a planner's question: how much payload can a booster place into orbit around Mars? Wagner considers both present and future booster systems, since Mars missions were then being planned years ahead.

He derives a simple method for calculating deliverable payload for named missions. The method works with arbitrary boosters and upper stage systems. Applying it, he finds present systems could put a few hundred pounds into favorable Mars orbits. Such payloads could observe conditions on and near Mars and relay the information home.
nasa-tm-19690005066-characteristics-of-c:
Frank R. Stevenson and Daniel J. Gauntner of Lewis Research Center checked carbon resistors used to measure high voltage in this report. A board of more than a thousand such resistors measured the end voltage of a large particle accelerator. True voltage values anchor each test run on such a machine.

The board was checked in place with known nuclear reactions and a magnet tool. After more than five years of hard use, its readings still matched the factory marks closely. Heat and voltage effects on resistance were also measured. Resistance fell in a straight line as voltage rose. The pair conclude such resistors and methods can be trusted for high voltage work.
nasa-tm-19690020379-a-136-mhz-ground-sta:
Ralph E. Taylor of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this April 1969 preprint, numbered X-523-69-135, on calibrating a satellite ground station. The station's receivers work at one hundred thirty-six megahertz. Instead of test gear alone, Taylor uses celestial noise sources: radio stars whose steady hiss gives a known reference signal from the sky itself.

Chapters walk through receiver setup, system noise temperature, and threshold sensitivity step by step. Two great radio sources, Cassiopeia A and Cygnus A, anchor the method. Trials with large dishes aimed at the galactic center are reported, in eighty-five-foot and forty-foot sizes. A final method turns the same radio stars to measuring antenna gain directly, with preliminary test data included.
nasa-tm-19700028217-mda-external-mobilit:
The Space Simulation and Experiments Office at the Marshall Space Flight Center issued this test report on September 12, 1969. It evaluates external mobility aids for the MDA, the multiple docking adapter. Astronauts working outside the craft would use the aids to move and hold position along its outer hull.

The test used neutral buoyancy, floating suited subjects in water to copy weightlessness. Its goal was a human factors judgment of the full external handrail system. Subjects found the handrail system usable, the abstract reports, and every docking port and airlock could be reached. Still, more handrails in key spots, especially around the cone section, would greatly ease an astronaut's moves.
nasa-tm-19710007891-spin-exchange-in-col:
G. M. Ressler and F. G. Major of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this paper in January 1971. It treats spin exchange in collisions between positive helium ions. When two such ions pass, an electron spin can swap between them, and the paper computes how likely that swap is.

The quantity sought is the spin exchange cross section, a measure of the collision's effective size for this effect. Ressler and Major calculate it in the impact parameter approximation, a way of sorting passes by closeness. A variational technique supplies the interaction potential between the two ions that the exchange creates. Sections on collision theory and the exchange interaction lead into their results and conclusions.
nasa-tm-19720012071-determination-of-ang:
John S. Preisser of the Langley Research Center wrote this memorandum in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2514, on recovering flight angles from tracking data. After a test flight, engineers know a vehicle's path from radar and its attitude from onboard gyroscopes. Combining the two should give angle of attack and sideslip, the angles between the vehicle and the air it moves through.

Preisser derives the needed equations for both rolling and nonrolling body axis systems, using a roll-stabilized gyro platform as the attitude source. The method assumes a flat, nonrotating Earth, a limit stated plainly in the summary. Sample calculations based on real flight data illustrate the method. Results from the gyro approach are compared with another technique that uses onboard camera data instead.
the-greatest-english-classic-a-study-of-: Cleland Boyd McAfee's study of the King James Bible as literature: its history, its language, and its shaping of English. the-life-and-legends-of-saint-francis-of: Father Candide Chalippe's biography gathers both the documented life and the beloved legends of Saint Francis of Assisi. The rich young man who gave up everything, preached to birds, and founded the Franciscan order comes alive through stories passed down for centuries. Reverent and richly detailed, it presents the saint as his devoted followers have cherished him.
